draft.h1: GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna: pricing, context, and fit
draft.intro: OpenAI introduced GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna as two GPT-6 API models with different capability-and-cost positioning. draft.what_changed: OpenAI introduced GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna. Sol is positioned for complex coding and agentic workflows at a lower unit cost than Astra, while Luna is positioned for focused, high-volume, and cost-sensitive workloads.
draft.why_it_matters: The two-model release creates a documented choice between a general-purpose tier for complex coding and agentic work and an efficiency-focused tier for cost-sensitive volume. Although they share the same stated context window, output limit, reasoning-effort settings, and input/output modalities, their standard token prices differ substantially. Teams can therefore evaluate workload fit and token economics separately from core context and modality requirements.

key_facts.claim: GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna are OpenAI GPT-6 models introduced together by OpenAI.
Both models have a 1,050,000-token context window and a maximum output of 128,000 tokens.
Both accept text and image input and produce text output.
Both models offer reasoning-effort settings of none, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max, with medium as the default.
Standard API pricing is $2 input, $0.20 cached input, $2.50 cache write, and $10 output per 1 million tokens for GPT-6 Sol; GPT-6 Luna is $0.10, $0.01, $0.125, and $0.50 respectively.

draft.pricing_or_capability_impact: Under standard API pricing, GPT-6 Luna is priced at $0.10 per 1 million input tokens and $0.50 per 1 million output tokens, versus $2 and $10 for GPT-6 Sol. Both models apply long-context pricing when total input exceeds 272,000 tokens: input, cached input, and cache-write prices are doubled, while output pricing is multiplied by 1.5 for the entire request. This makes request-level input size relevant when estimating costs, even though both models list a 1.05 million-token context window.

comparison_points.analysis: GPT-6 Sol is positioned as a general-purpose GPT-6 tier for complex coding and agentic workflows. GPT-6 Luna is positioned as an efficiency-focused tier for focused, high-volume, and cost-sensitive workloads.
Per 1 million tokens, GPT-6 Sol lists $2 input, $0.20 cached input, $2.50 cache write, and $10 output. GPT-6 Luna lists $0.10 input, $0.01 cached input, $0.125 cache write, and $0.50 output.

Both GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna list a 1,050,000-token context window and a 128,000-token maximum output. Context capacity and output ceiling therefore do not distinguish the two based on the documented specifications.
GPT-6 Sol lists a knowledge cutoff of 2026-04-20. GPT-6 Luna lists a knowledge cutoff of 2026-05-18.
Both models accept text and image input, return text output, and offer the same documented reasoning-effort levels from none through max, with medium as default.

technical_details.detail: GPT-6 Sol has a 1,050,000-token context window, 128,000-token maximum output, and a listed knowledge cutoff of 2026-04-20.
GPT-6 Luna has a 1,050,000-token context window, 128,000-token maximum output, and a listed knowledge cutoff of 2026-05-18.
GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna accept text and image input, produce text output, and support reasoning effort of none, low, medium, high, xhigh, or max; medium is the documented default.
For each model, when total input exceeds 272,000 tokens, long-context pricing applies to the entire request: input, cached input, and cache-write multipliers are 2×, while output is 1.5×.

practical_takeaways.takeaway: Choose GPT-6 Sol when the documented target workload is complex coding or agentic work; choose GPT-6 Luna when the workload is focused, high-volume, or cost-sensitive.
Do not select between Sol and Luna based on listed context capacity, maximum output, text/image input, or text output: those documented specifications are the same for both models.
Estimate costs using the appropriate token category—input, cached input, cache write, and output—and account for the long-context rule when total input exceeds 272,000 tokens.
For volume-sensitive workloads, compare expected input and output mix rather than input pricing alone, because Sol and Luna have separate rates for input, cached input, cache write, and output.

draft.who_should_care: API teams choosing between an OpenAI model for complex coding or agentic workflows and one for focused, high-volume, or cost-sensitive work should compare GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna. Teams handling large prompts should also review the documented long-context pricing rule, which applies once total input exceeds 272,000 tokens.

Estimate input, cached-input, cache-write, and output token volumes for the intended workload.
Check whether requests can exceed 272,000 total input tokens, because long-context pricing applies to the entire request above that threshold.
Validate the model against the specific coding, agentic, focused, or high-volume task before selecting a production default.

draft.h1: GitHub Copilot in VS Code: September 2026 agent updates
draft.intro: GitHub’s September 2026 Copilot releases for Visual Studio Code, spanning VS Code 1.136 through 1.140, pushed the Agents window beyond interactive coding toward a fuller agent workflow. The month added scheduled automations, agent-assisted pull request merge work, Dev Container sessions, HydraFusion orchestration, richer GitHub context, and continuity between ChatGPT Codex conversations and VS Code.
draft.what_changed: Across VS Code 1.136 through 1.140, GitHub added a sequence of agent-workflow features rather than one isolated Copilot update. Agent Merge entered public preview to handle review feedback, failed checks, merge conflicts, and workflow reruns. Automations added hourly, daily, weekly, and on-demand recurring tasks. Dev Container sessions brought project-configured tools and dependencies into the Agents window, pull requests could be created directly from Copilot, Claude, or Codex sessions, and HydraFusion reached VS Code as a research preview for selecting multi-model workflows.
draft.why_it_matters: The September releases move GitHub Copilot closer to an end-to-end development workflow that can keep context across implementation, environment setup, pull request creation, review, checks, and follow-up work. For developers, the important change is not a single model upgrade; it is the growing coordination layer around agents. For engineering leads, that makes preview status, permissions, environment configuration, review policy, and automation scope more important because the agent can participate in more stages of the software delivery loop.

key_facts.claim: GitHub’s September 2026 VS Code recap covers versions 1.136 through 1.140 and centers on agent-driven development from implementation through pull request merge.
Agent Merge can handle review feedback, failed checks, merge conflicts, and workflow reruns from an active agent session; GitHub labels the feature preview in the September recap.
VS Code automations can run recurring agent tasks hourly, daily, or weekly, or run them on demand; the feature was introduced in public preview during the September release sequence.
HydraFusion reached VS Code as a research preview and can choose among single, cascade, and critique workflows that coordinate model use within a task.
The Agents window can start sessions in Dev Containers using project-configured tools and dependencies, including supported remote scenarios such as SSH, Tunnel, and WSL hosts.
Developers can create pull requests from Copilot, Claude, or Codex agent sessions in the Agents window after reviewing and editing the pull request details.
VS Code can continue a Codex conversation started in the ChatGPT app, bringing that conversation into the codebase without manually copying context or files.
GitHub issues and pull requests can be attached as context to Copilot chats, and active chats are no longer interrupted when another agent message arrives.

draft.pricing_or_capability_impact: This release sequence is primarily a capability and workflow expansion. GitHub is giving Copilot agents more ways to schedule work, operate inside project environments, create and advance pull requests, carry context across sessions and applications, and coordinate model workflows. The practical impact depends on which preview features a user or organization enables and how much authority teams allow agents to exercise around repositories, checks, and pull requests.

comparison_points.analysis: Agent Merge entered public preview, giving agent sessions a path to address review feedback, failed checks, and merge conflicts while session organization also improved.
Automations entered public preview for recurring agent tasks on hourly, daily, or weekly schedules, with on-demand execution also available.
The Agents window added local Dev Container sessions and direct pull request creation from agent sessions, extending agents into project environments and delivery workflow.
HydraFusion expanded into VS Code as a research preview, adding workflow-level orchestration that can choose single, cascade, or critique execution patterns.

technical_details.detail: Agent Merge monitors the pull request loop: the September recap says it can address review feedback, failed checks, merge conflicts, and rerun workflows from an active session.
Automations support hourly, daily, and weekly schedules as well as on-demand runs, allowing recurring prompts to become repeatable agent tasks.
HydraFusion is available in VS Code 1.140 or later as a research preview and uses single, cascade, or critique workflows instead of behaving like one fixed model.
Dev Container agent sessions use the project’s configured tools and dependencies; GitHub’s weekly release notes say the rollout requires Docker and a supported Dev Container configuration.
Codex conversations can move from the ChatGPT app into VS Code, while GitHub issues or pull requests can be attached directly as chat context.

GitHub’s account of its Copilot runtime migration describes Agent Merge handling pull request follow-up such as CI failures, review comments, and conflicts while engineers still retained final review judgment.

practical_takeaways.takeaway: Treat the September release as a workflow change, not only a chat feature update: evaluate where Copilot can now enter your implementation, review, CI, and pull request process.

Separate stable capabilities from preview and research-preview features before standardizing them across a team; Agent Merge, automations, cleanup features, and HydraFusion have different maturity labels.

Use automations for recurring repository work only after defining the prompt, target repository, cadence, and review expectations clearly, because the task can repeat without a fresh manual start each time.
For Dev Container sessions, verify that the repository’s container configuration and required tools are suitable for the agent workflow before relying on it as the team default.
Keep human review boundaries explicit around pull request completion. GitHub’s own runtime-migration write-up describes engineers spot-checking Agent Merge results before final merge decisions.

draft.who_should_care: VS Code developers using GitHub Copilot agents, engineering leads managing pull request and CI workflows, platform teams maintaining Dev Container environments, and organizations deciding which preview agent capabilities to enable should care most. The release affects how work is scheduled, how agents receive repository context, how sessions move across environments and apps, and how far an agent can participate in the pull request lifecycle.
what_to_verify: Confirm the VS Code version required for the feature you plan to use; HydraFusion specifically requires VS Code 1.140 or later according to GitHub’s release note.
Check whether preview or research-preview features are enabled for your Copilot plan and whether an organization or enterprise administrator must allow them.
Validate the repository and permission scope used by automations and Agent Merge before enabling recurring or pull-request-changing workflows.
For Dev Container sessions, confirm Docker availability and that the repository has a supported Dev Container configuration with the required tools and dependencies.
Test how your team wants humans to review agent changes, CI fixes, review responses, and final merge decisions before making Agent Merge part of a standard delivery process.

faq.answer: GitHub’s September recap covers VS Code 1.136 through 1.140 and adds scheduled automations, Agent Merge, pull request creation from agent sessions, Dev Container sessions, HydraFusion, better session organization, GitHub issue and pull request context, and cross-app Codex continuity.

draft.h1: GPT-6.1 Sol: pricing, specs, benchmarks and availability
draft.intro: GPT-6.1 Sol is OpenAI’s upgraded Sol model for complex coding, computer use, professional work, and agentic workflows. It keeps the Sol price tier for standard input and output tokens while cutting cached-input cost, adds stronger benchmark performance across several demanding tasks, and is positioned as the lower-cost alternative when teams want performance closer to GPT-6 Astra without paying Astra’s standard token rates.
draft.what_changed: OpenAI introduced GPT-6.1 Sol on September 29, 2026 as an upgrade to GPT-6 Sol. The new model targets the same broad class of demanding coding and agentic work but improves capability across software engineering, professional document tasks, multi-step business workflows, computer use, scientific workflows, factuality, and alignment evaluations. OpenAI also cut cached-input pricing from GPT-6 Sol’s documented $0.20 per million tokens to $0.10 for GPT-6.1 Sol while keeping standard input at $2 and output at $10 per million tokens.
draft.why_it_matters: GPT-6.1 Sol changes the model-selection tradeoff inside the GPT-6 family. Teams that previously had to choose between GPT-6 Sol’s lower cost and GPT-6 Astra’s stronger performance now have a model OpenAI says approaches Astra on several complex workloads at materially lower cost. The release is especially relevant for agents that reuse large amounts of context, because cached input is cheaper than on GPT-6 Sol, and for production teams that need tool calling, computer use, code execution, MCP, or long-context work without moving to Astra pricing.

key_facts.claim: OpenAI introduced GPT-6.1 Sol on September 29, 2026 as the latest model family update in the GPT-6 series and described it as an upgrade to GPT-6 Sol.
GPT-6.1 Sol has a 1,050,000-token context window, supports up to 128,000 output tokens, and lists an April 30, 2026 knowledge cutoff.
Standard API pricing is $2 per million input tokens, $0.10 per million cached input tokens, and $10 per million output tokens.
Compared with GPT-6 Sol, GPT-6.1 Sol keeps the same documented standard input and output price points while reducing cached-input pricing from $0.20 to $0.10 per million tokens.
GPT-6.1 Sol supports low, medium, high, xhigh, and max reasoning effort, with medium documented as the default; none and minimal are not supported.
OpenAI documents support for web search, file search, image generation, code interpreter, hosted shell, apply patch, skills, computer use, MCP, and tool search through the Responses API tool stack.
GPT-6.1 Sol is available through the OpenAI API as gpt-6.1-sol and is also available in ChatGPT Work and Codex for eligible paid-plan users, subject to plan and workspace access.

OpenAI’s deployment safety addendum classifies GPT-6.1 Sol as Critical for cybersecurity capability and High for biological and chemical capability under its Preparedness Framework, and says it uses the same safeguards stack as GPT-6 Astra.

draft.pricing_or_capability_impact: At standard API rates, GPT-6.1 Sol costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens versus $10 and $50 for GPT-6 Astra in OpenAI’s launch comparison. That is one-fifth of Astra’s standard input and output token prices. Cached input is $0.10 per million tokens for GPT-6.1 Sol, compared with $0.20 for GPT-6 Sol and $1.00 for Astra in the same launch material. For agent workflows that repeatedly reuse context, the cached-input reduction can matter independently of the headline input/output rates.

comparison_points.dimension: GPT-6.1 Sol vs GPT-6 Sol — coding
comparison_points.analysis: On DeepSWE v1.1, OpenAI reports that GPT-6.1 Sol matches GPT-6 Astra at roughly one-fifth of the cost and exceeds GPT-6 Sol’s best score by 6.4 percentage points at a lower reasoning effort and cost.
On GDP.pdf, OpenAI reports that GPT-6.1 Sol approaches GPT-6 Astra’s performance at roughly one-fifth the cost per task and scores above Opus 5.5 with fallbacks across the tested reasoning settings.
On AutomationBench, GPT-6.1 Sol is reported 4.8 percentage points above GPT-6 Sol at the same medium reasoning setting and 2.2 points above Opus 5.5 at roughly one-third of the cost.

On the OSWorld 2.0 offline set, OpenAI reports GPT-6.1 Sol seven percentage points above GPT-6 Sol at maximum reasoning effort, while coming within 2.1 points of Astra at roughly one-seventh the cost per task.

On Terminal-Bench Science 0.1, OpenAI reports that GPT-6.1 Sol more than doubles GPT-6 Sol’s score at maximum reasoning effort and costs $5.47 per task on average at that setting, versus $23.80 for Astra; Astra still posts the highest score at 68.1%.

In OpenAI’s difficult factuality evaluation, GPT-6.1 Sol reduces the share of responses containing a factual error from 11.4% with GPT-6 Sol to 7.7% at low reasoning effort, while staying within 1.9 percentage points of Astra across tested reasoning settings.

technical_details.detail: Use model ID gpt-6.1-sol in the API. OpenAI recommends the Responses API for tool calling; Chat Completions is supported for requests without tools.

The model supports a 1.05 million-token context window and up to 128,000 output tokens, making it suitable for long-document, codebase, and multi-step agent workloads where large working context matters.
Reasoning effort can be set to low, medium, high, xhigh, or max. Medium is the documented default, while none and minimal are not supported for GPT-6.1 Sol.

The documented tool set includes function calling, web search, file search, image generation, code interpreter, hosted shell, apply patch, skills, computer use, MCP, and tool search when using the supported API path.
GPT-6.1 Sol supports structured outputs and streaming but does not support fine-tuning according to the current model documentation.
OpenAI documents US and EU data residency for GPT-6.1 Sol, with availability and processing-mode details subject to the data-residency rules described in its API documentation.

practical_takeaways.takeaway: Benchmark GPT-6.1 Sol against Astra on your own complex tasks rather than assuming the cheaper model is always sufficient; OpenAI itself recommends comparing the quality-versus-cost tradeoff on real workloads.

For agent systems that reuse large prompts, files, or instructions across requests, include cached-input volume in cost estimates because GPT-6.1 Sol’s $0.10 cached-input rate is half GPT-6 Sol’s documented rate.

Use the Responses API when the workflow requires tools such as computer use, web search, hosted shell, code interpreter, MCP, or apply patch; do not design a tool-heavy deployment around Chat Completions for this model.

Do not migrate from GPT-6 Sol only on benchmark headlines. Validate latency, reasoning-effort settings, tool behavior, factuality, and total cost per completed task under the same prompts and environment your production system uses.

For Work or Codex deployments, verify plan eligibility and workspace permissions before standardizing GPT-6.1 Sol as a team default, because model availability can depend on rollout access and administrator settings.

draft.who_should_care: API teams running coding or agent workflows, developers using computer-use or tool-calling systems, organizations processing complex professional documents, and Work or Codex users choosing between Sol and Astra should care most. GPT-6.1 Sol is particularly relevant when the workload needs more capability than GPT-6 Sol but the cost profile of Astra is difficult to justify at production scale.
what_to_verify: Confirm that gpt-6.1-sol is enabled for the API project, ChatGPT plan, or workspace where you intend to deploy it.
Benchmark GPT-6.1 Sol against both GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Astra using the same prompts, tools, reasoning effort, and acceptance criteria used in production.
Estimate standard input, cached input, and output separately; repeated-context agent workloads may benefit disproportionately from the lower cached-input price.
Check whether your workflow requires tool calling, because OpenAI directs GPT-6.1 Sol tool use through the Responses API rather than Chat Completions.
Review the current model and safety documentation for residency, safeguard, and capability restrictions before deploying high-impact or security-sensitive agent workflows.

signal.summary: You can now read, add, and edit comments on repository security advisories using the REST API, including advisories created from private vulnerability reports.

draft.seo_title: GitHub Security Advisory Comments API: Public Preview
draft.meta_description: GitHub’s REST API can now list, read, add and edit repository security advisory comments. See permissions, confidential limits, use cases and rollout.
draft.h1: GitHub repository security advisory comments API: public preview
draft.intro: GitHub’s repository security advisory comments API brings advisory discussion into the REST API for the first time. Security teams can now list, retrieve, add, and edit non-confidential comments on repository security advisories, including advisories created from private vulnerability reports. The change matters because triage context, coordination notes, audit evidence, and migration data no longer have to remain locked inside the web interface.
draft.what_changed: Before this public preview, repository security advisory discussion was available through GitHub’s web interface but not exposed through a comparable REST comments workflow. GitHub now provides REST operations to list advisory comments, fetch an individual comment, add a comment, and edit an existing comment. List operations can be limited to comments updated since a given time, and repository advisory responses now expose a comments count. GitHub also adds the linked repository-advisory comment count to global advisory responses so tools can detect active discussion before fetching comment bodies.
draft.why_it_matters: Repository security advisories often contain the operational context that does not fit neatly into CVE metadata: questions from reporters, triage decisions, reproduction details, coordination status, and follow-up notes. REST access means that context can participate in the same automation patterns teams already use around issues and pull requests. Security engineering teams can export discussions for audits or migrations, add triage notes from internal tooling, identify advisories with active discussion, and build workflows around private vulnerability reports without requiring a person to copy information out of the GitHub web UI.

key_facts.claim: The public-preview API can list comments on a repository security advisory, retrieve one comment, add a comment, and edit a comment.
The list operation can be limited to comments updated since a specified time, which supports incremental synchronization instead of repeatedly pulling an entire discussion history.

Repository security advisory responses now include a comments count, and global advisory responses include the count for their linked repository advisory; GitHub says these counts cover non-confidential comments.
The REST comments API also works with repository security advisories created from private vulnerability reports, so reporter discussions can be integrated into automated triage workflows.

Access follows the advisory’s permissions. A caller must be able to view the advisory and have the appropriate repository security advisories read or write permission or token scope for the action being performed.
Confidential comments are not returned by these REST endpoints. GitHub exposes confidential comments separately through GraphQL, and repository collaborators without write access cannot read them.
Deleting advisory comments is not supported through the REST API in this public preview.
GitHub says the comments API preview is available for public repositories on GitHub Free, GitHub Pro, GitHub Team, and GitHub Enterprise Cloud.

draft.pricing_or_capability_impact: This release changes workflow capability rather than pricing. Security tooling can now treat repository-advisory discussion as structured API data instead of browser-only context. That enables incremental synchronization, audit exports, migration tooling, automated triage notes, and advisory dashboards that first inspect comment counts before fetching discussion content. The main boundary is confidentiality: REST exposes non-confidential discussion only, while confidential maintainer comments remain outside this REST surface.

comparison_points.analysis: Previously, the discussion attached to a repository security advisory was primarily reachable through the web interface. The preview adds REST operations to list advisory comments and retrieve a single comment.
Security automation can now add comments and edit existing comments through the REST API, making it possible for internal triage systems to write notes back to an advisory.

Repository advisory responses now include a non-confidential comment count, and linked repository-advisory counts also appear in global advisory responses. Tools can use the count to decide whether a discussion fetch is necessary.
When a private vulnerability report becomes a draft repository security advisory, its regular discussion can participate in the same comments API workflow, subject to the advisory’s access rules.

Confidential comments remain deliberately separated from the REST surface. They are limited to people with repository write access and are available through GraphQL rather than the new REST comments endpoints.
The preview supports reading, creating, and editing comments but does not yet support deleting them through the REST API.

technical_details.detail: A synchronization job can request advisory comments updated since a given time, which lets an integration process only changed discussion instead of treating every advisory thread as a full refresh.

Authorization is inherited from the repository security advisory model: callers must be able to access the advisory and use a token or app permission appropriate for repository security advisories and the requested read or write action.

The comments count exposed on advisory responses counts non-confidential comments. It should not be interpreted as the complete number of all maintainer-visible comments when confidential discussion exists.

Confidential comments are permission-sensitive maintainer notes. They are visible only to people with repository write access, are not returned by the REST comments API, and views of them are recorded in GitHub’s audit log.

Private vulnerability reports can become draft repository security advisories. Regular comments are visible to the reporter and advisory collaborators, while confidential comments provide a separate maintainer-only discussion channel.
The preview is scoped to public repositories across GitHub Free, Pro, Team, and Enterprise Cloud according to GitHub’s release announcement.

practical_takeaways.takeaway: Use the comments count as a cheap discovery signal before fetching discussion bodies when building organization-wide advisory dashboards or migration tooling.

For audit or archival pipelines, synchronize comments incrementally with the updated-since filter and store advisory identifiers alongside comment records so the discussion remains traceable to its source advisory.

Do not assume REST exports contain every maintainer discussion. If confidential comments are in use, design the audit process around the fact that those comments are intentionally omitted from the REST endpoints.
Separate read-only integrations from tools that add or edit triage notes, and grant only the repository security advisories permission level required for the workflow.

If a workflow depends on deleting comments or changing a comment between regular and confidential, account for current limitations: REST deletion is not supported, and GitHub does not let a posted comment switch confidentiality state.

draft.who_should_care: Application security teams, open-source maintainers, vulnerability-management platform builders, security operations teams, auditors, and organizations migrating advisory data should care most. The API is especially useful when repository security advisories are part of a larger security workflow and the discussion itself contains triage context that must be synchronized, analyzed, archived, or updated by internal tooling.
what_to_verify: Confirm that the target repository and plan are covered by the current public-preview rollout before depending on the comments endpoints in production automation.
Verify the exact repository security advisories read or write permission required by the token or GitHub App for each operation your integration performs.
Treat the advisory comment count as a count of non-confidential discussion, not a guarantee that every maintainer-only note is represented.
If the workflow handles private vulnerability reports, test access using the same reporter, collaborator, maintainer, and app permission roles that will exist in production.
Design around the current no-delete limitation for REST comments and decide how your system will handle corrections that cannot be represented as deletion.

faq.question: What can the GitHub repository security advisory comments API do?
faq.answer: In public preview, the REST API can list comments on a repository security advisory, get a single comment, add a comment, and edit a comment. GitHub also supports filtering listed comments by update time.

faq.question: Does the comments API work with private vulnerability reports?
faq.answer: Yes. GitHub says the REST comments endpoints work with repository security advisories created from private vulnerability reports, subject to the same access rules that control the advisory itself.

faq.question: Can the REST API return confidential advisory comments?
faq.answer: No. GitHub states that confidential comments are not returned by the new REST comments endpoints. Confidential comments are maintainer-only, require repository write access, and are available separately through GraphQL.

faq.question: What permissions are required for security advisory comments?
faq.answer: A caller must be able to view the repository security advisory and have the appropriate repository security advisories read or write permission or token scope for the operation. Users who cannot access the advisory cannot access its comments.

faq.question: Can repository security advisory comments be deleted through the REST API?
faq.answer: Not in the current public preview. GitHub supports listing, reading, adding, and editing comments through these REST endpoints, but deleting comments is not yet supported.

faq.question: Which GitHub plans have the advisory comments API preview?
faq.answer: GitHub says the public preview is available for public repositories on GitHub Free, GitHub Pro, GitHub Team, and GitHub Enterprise Cloud.

signal.title: Actions Runner Controller release 0.15.0
signal.summary: GitHub Actions Runner Controller 0.15.0 includes reliability, scalability, and observability improvements for runner scale sets. These updates help you operate larger runner fleets with fewer disruptions during upgrades and Kubernetes…

draft.seo_title: Actions Runner Controller 0.15.0: Upgrade & Scale Changes
draft.meta_description: ARC 0.15.0 improves in-place upgrades, graceful shutdowns, metrics, Kubernetes API load, concurrency and runner cleanup for scale sets.
draft.h1: Actions Runner Controller 0.15.0: reliability, scale and upgrade changes
draft.intro: Actions Runner Controller 0.15.0 is a Kubernetes-focused reliability and scalability release for GitHub Actions runner scale sets. Instead of adding a new runner model, it changes how ARC upgrades resources, shuts down controllers, re-registers missing scale sets, reports runner state, talks to the Kubernetes API, controls reconciliation concurrency, and cleans up completed ephemeral runners. Those changes matter most to teams operating larger self-hosted runner fleets.
draft.what_changed: GitHub’s 0.15.0 release concentrates on controller behavior under scale and during lifecycle transitions. Patch-version upgrades can update runner-set resources in place, controller shutdown timing can be aligned with Kubernetes termination grace periods, and a scale set can be registered again when ARC’s recorded set no longer exists in the Actions service. The controller also shifts several high-frequency operations away from full object updates and status patches, adds configurable Kubernetes client rate limits and reconciliation concurrency, filters more incoming events, and shortens cleanup for successfully exited ephemeral runners.
draft.why_it_matters: ARC is the Kubernetes-based reference implementation GitHub recommends for autoscaling self-hosted runner scale sets, so controller overhead becomes an operational concern as fleets grow. Version 0.15.0 targets the control-plane work that can create disruption or unnecessary Kubernetes API traffic: upgrades, reconciliation loops, listener request rates, status writes, graceful shutdowns, and runner cleanup. For platform teams, the practical value is a controller that can spend less time rewriting state and more predictably handle large numbers of scale sets without changing how workflows target those runners.

key_facts.claim: GitHub describes Actions Runner Controller 0.15.0 as a reliability, scalability, and observability release for runner scale sets, with an emphasis on larger fleets and fewer disruptions during upgrades and Kubernetes API updates.
Patch-version upgrades can now update resources in place, reducing disruption between AutoscalingRunnerSet and EphemeralRunnerSet resources during upgrades.
Controller shutdown behavior can be aligned by configuring terminationGracePeriodSeconds to match the controller manager graceful-shutdown timeout.
ARC can re-register a runner scale set when the scale set recorded by the controller no longer exists in the GitHub Actions service.
Controller writes now use Kubernetes patch requests instead of full update requests for relevant operations, reducing API payload size.
Runner status aggregation for EphemeralRunnerSet and AutoscalingRunnerSet moves to metrics, reducing status patch requests against the Kubernetes API.
Listener Kubernetes client QPS and burst limits are configurable, and controller reconciliation concurrency can be configured globally or per controller with max-concurrent-reconciles flags.
GitHub only supports the latest Autoscaling Runner Sets version of ARC; legacy community-maintained ARC remains community-supported rather than GitHub-supported.

draft.pricing_or_capability_impact: ARC 0.15.0 does not introduce a new GitHub Actions price model. Its impact is operational: fewer disruptive resource replacements during applicable upgrades, smaller Kubernetes API writes, fewer status patches, tunable listener request rates, configurable reconciliation parallelism, and faster deletion of successfully exited ephemeral runners. Those controls can matter when runner capacity is already large enough that API pressure, reconcile throughput, shutdown timing, and stale resource state become part of normal platform operations.

comparison_points.analysis: Patch-version upgrades can update runner-set resources in place instead of creating avoidable replacement churn between autoscaling and ephemeral runner sets, reducing upgrade disruption.
terminationGracePeriodSeconds can be configured so Kubernetes pod termination and the controller manager’s graceful-shutdown timeout are aligned rather than competing timers.
ARC 0.15.0 uses patch requests instead of full update requests for controller updates and moves runner status aggregation toward metrics, lowering payload size and status-write volume.
Kubernetes client QPS and burst settings for listeners are configurable, giving operators a way to tune how aggressively listeners communicate with the Kubernetes API.
Global and per-controller max-concurrent-reconciles settings let operators tune controller concurrency, while event filtering reduces reconciliations triggered by changes that do not require work.
When a runner pod exits successfully, ARC can delete the ephemeral runner faster because it skips a server-side check for runner removal.

technical_details.detail: ARC runner scale sets are Kubernetes-managed pools of homogeneous GitHub Actions runners that can autoscale with workload demand; workflows target the runner scale set by its configured name or labels.

ARC exposes Prometheus-format metrics from controller-manager and listener pods. GitHub’s documentation lists controller metrics for pending, running, and failed ephemeral runners and listener metrics for assigned jobs, running jobs, registered runners, busy runners, desired runners, and job timing.

Version 0.15.0 reduces dependence on Kubernetes status patching by moving EphemeralRunnerSet and AutoscalingRunnerSet runner-state aggregation into metrics, which is relevant for clusters where status-write volume contributes to API-server load.
The release adds configurable listener Kubernetes-client QPS and burst settings so high-scale deployments can tune request behavior instead of relying only on fixed client defaults.
Controller reconciliation can be tuned globally or per controller through max-concurrent-reconciles flags, giving operators a direct control over how many reconciliations can progress concurrently.

GitHub recommends retaining logs from the ARC controller, listeners, and ephemeral runners, which becomes especially important when operators tune concurrency, client rates, or lifecycle behavior and need evidence for troubleshooting.

practical_takeaways.takeaway: Treat 0.15.0 as an operations-focused upgrade: measure upgrade disruption, Kubernetes API request behavior, reconcile latency, listener health, and runner cleanup before and after rollout instead of judging it only by job throughput.

If controller pods sometimes terminate before reconciliation work finishes, review terminationGracePeriodSeconds alongside the controller manager graceful-shutdown timeout so Kubernetes and ARC use compatible shutdown windows.

For large fleets, watch API-server load and ARC metrics before increasing QPS, burst, or max-concurrent-reconciles. Higher concurrency can improve throughput, but it should be tuned against the capacity and rate behavior of the cluster.
Confirm that observability is enabled before rollout so you can compare runner-state metrics and controller behavior after the move away from frequent status aggregation patches.

Use the GitHub-supported Autoscaling Runner Sets line for production support expectations and verify the deployed chart version explicitly; GitHub documents support for the latest Autoscaling Runner Sets release rather than legacy ARC.

draft.who_should_care: Platform engineering teams operating GitHub Actions on Kubernetes, organizations with many runner scale sets, SRE teams responsible for Kubernetes API health, and developers maintaining internal self-hosted runner platforms should care most. The release is less about visible workflow features and more about reducing control-plane friction as ARC installations become larger, more concurrent, and more sensitive to upgrade and reconciliation behavior.
what_to_verify: Confirm the exact gha-runner-scale-set-controller and gha-runner-scale-set chart versions deployed in each cluster before planning the upgrade.
Review existing terminationGracePeriodSeconds values and controller shutdown settings so graceful shutdown behavior is intentionally aligned after the upgrade.
Capture baseline Kubernetes API request rates, ARC controller metrics, listener metrics, reconciliation latency, and runner cleanup behavior before changing QPS, burst, or concurrency settings.

Test the upgrade on a representative runner scale set and confirm that in-place resource changes do not conflict with custom labels, annotations, sidecars, runner modes, or admission policies used in your cluster.
Verify that logs from controller, listener, and ephemeral runner pods are retained so failures introduced by scale or lifecycle tuning can be diagnosed after pods are replaced.

faq.question: What changed in Actions Runner Controller 0.15.0?
faq.answer: ARC 0.15.0 focuses on reliability and scale: in-place patch-version upgrades, more predictable graceful shutdowns, scale-set re-registration, smaller Kubernetes API writes, metrics-based runner status aggregation, configurable listener rate limits, tunable reconciliation concurrency, event filtering, and faster ephemeral runner cleanup.

faq.question: Does ARC 0.15.0 reduce disruption during upgrades?
faq.answer: Yes for the upgrade path GitHub describes. Patch-version upgrades can update resources in place, reducing disruption between autoscaling runner sets and ephemeral runner sets compared with replacement-heavy behavior.

faq.question: How does ARC 0.15.0 reduce Kubernetes API load?
faq.answer: The release uses patch requests instead of full update requests for controller changes, moves runner-status aggregation to metrics for key runner-set resources, filters more incoming events, and lets operators configure listener QPS and burst settings.

faq.question: What does max-concurrent-reconciles change in ARC?
faq.answer: The new global and per-controller max-concurrent-reconciles controls let operators tune how many reconciliation loops can execute at the same time. This is primarily a controller-throughput and cluster-load tuning mechanism.

faq.question: Who should prioritize the ARC 0.15.0 upgrade?
faq.answer: Teams running larger Kubernetes-based GitHub Actions runner fleets should evaluate it first, especially if they experience upgrade disruption, heavy Kubernetes API traffic, reconcile bottlenecks, listener pressure, or slow ephemeral-runner cleanup.

faq.question: Is Actions Runner Controller the supported Kubernetes autoscaling option for GitHub Actions?
faq.answer: GitHub documents Autoscaling Runner Sets in ARC as its supported Kubernetes-based runner autoscaling line and states that only the latest Autoscaling Runner Sets version is supported by GitHub; legacy ARC remains community-supported.

draft.seo_title: Higgsfield + GPT-6 Astra: Video Features in One Day
draft.meta_description: Higgsfield says one engineer shipped new video exploration features in a day with GPT-6 Astra. See the workflow, model role, costs, limits, and lessons.
draft.h1: How Higgsfield used GPT-6 Astra to ship video features in a day
draft.intro: Higgsfield AI’s GPT-6 Astra case study is useful for two different reasons: it describes a customer-facing workflow that turns an existing video ad into many new creative directions, and an internal engineering workflow where Higgsfield says one engineer delivered new exploration features within a day. The key detail is that Astra is supporting planning, reasoning, and development around a video product—not acting as the video-generation model itself.
draft.what_changed: OpenAI says Higgsfield is using GPT-6 Astra on both sides of its product workflow. For customers, a prompt such as taking a top-performing ad and generating 100 new variations can be turned into new creative directions, including localized versions for different countries. Inside Higgsfield, the company says Astra’s long-horizon task planning and ability to plan across multiple steps helped a single engineer bring new exploration features to market within a day, working closely with the creative team.
draft.why_it_matters: The case study illustrates a broader pattern for multimodal products: the highest-value language model may sit above the media-generation layer, coordinating intent, planning variations, structuring multi-step work, and helping engineers build product capabilities faster. That is different from claiming the model generates the final video. OpenAI’s own GPT-6 Astra model page lists video input and video output as unsupported, so the evidence points to Astra as a reasoning and workflow component inside Higgsfield’s broader video stack.

key_facts.claim: OpenAI published the Higgsfield case study on September 21, 2026 and says GPT-6 Astra supports both customer-facing ad creation and faster feature development inside Higgsfield.

Higgsfield’s example customer workflow starts with an instruction such as taking a top-performing ad and generating 100 new variations, with possible creative directions including versions customized for different countries.
Higgsfield CEO Alex Mashrabov says GPT-6 Astra helped a single engineer deliver new exploration features within a day.

OpenAI attributes the internal development speed in the case study to Astra’s long-horizon task planning, multi-step planning capability, and collaboration between Higgsfield’s creative and engineering teams.
GPT-6 Astra’s official model documentation lists text and image input with text output; audio and video input or output are not supported by the model itself.
GPT-6 Astra has a 1,050,000-token context window, supports up to 128,000 output tokens, and lists an April 30, 2026 knowledge cutoff.
Standard GPT-6 Astra API pricing is $10 per million input tokens, $1 per million cached input tokens, $12.50 per million cache-write tokens, and $50 per million output tokens.
OpenAI positions GPT-6 Astra for demanding reasoning, coding, computer use, research, and professional work, with reasoning effort settings from low through max.

draft.pricing_or_capability_impact: The Higgsfield story does not disclose token usage, reasoning-effort settings, per-feature API cost, engineering hours saved against a measured baseline, or the cost of the video-generation layer. For teams evaluating a similar architecture, Astra’s standard API rates are $10 per million input tokens, $1 cached input, $12.50 cache write, and $50 output. Requests above 272,000 input tokens use higher long-context rates for the full request, so the economics of a large-context creative or coding workflow depend heavily on prompt size, cache reuse, output volume, and how often the workflow runs.

comparison_points.analysis: The customer workflow uses GPT-6 to turn a high-level ad request into creative directions and variations. The case study gives country customization as an example of how one existing ad can branch into many versions.

Higgsfield says GPT-6 Astra helps a single engineer deliver new exploration features within a day, with OpenAI highlighting long-horizon and multi-step planning rather than a narrow code-completion task.

GPT-6 Astra should not be interpreted as Higgsfield’s video-generation engine. OpenAI’s model page lists video input and video output as unsupported, while the case study describes Astra supporting creative-direction and engineering workflows around Higgsfield’s video product.

The one-day result is a Higgsfield-reported customer outcome quoted in OpenAI’s case study. The page does not provide an independent benchmark, a pre-Astra engineering baseline, task complexity measurements, or a controlled comparison with another model.

Astra is positioned by OpenAI for demanding multi-step reasoning, coding, computer use, and professional work, which aligns with the case study’s description of long-horizon planning and feature-development assistance.

OpenAI publishes Astra’s API token prices, but the Higgsfield case study does not disclose the number of tokens, tool calls, reasoning effort, cache behavior, or total model spend behind either the ad workflow or the one-day engineering result.

technical_details.detail: GPT-6 Astra’s model ID is gpt-6-astra. Its documented context window is 1.05 million tokens with a maximum output of 128,000 tokens, which can support large project context and multi-step work when the application supplies that context.

The model accepts text and image input and returns text output. OpenAI explicitly marks video input and video output as unsupported, which is important when interpreting Astra’s role in a video-production company.

Astra supports low, medium, high, xhigh, and max reasoning effort. OpenAI’s model guidance recommends choosing model and reasoning effort based on workload quality, latency, and cost rather than assuming the highest setting is required for every task.
Through the Responses API, GPT-6 Astra supports tools including web search, file search, image generation, code interpreter, hosted shell, apply patch, skills, computer use, MCP, and tool search.
For prompts above 272,000 input tokens, OpenAI documents long-context pricing that doubles input and cache rates and multiplies output pricing by 1.5 for the full request.

OpenAI’s GPT-6 guidance describes Astra as capable of multi-step workflows across code, browsers, and professional software, which is consistent with the planning-oriented role described in the Higgsfield case study.

practical_takeaways.takeaway: Separate the orchestration model from the media-generation model in your architecture. A strong reasoning model can plan creative variants, analyze inputs, coordinate steps, or help build product features without being the system that renders the final video.

When evaluating a one-day development claim, reproduce the same feature with a documented baseline: task scope, engineer time, prompts, tool access, review time, failures, and final acceptance criteria should all be measured.
For customer-facing creative variation, test whether the model improves useful variation quality and localization rather than merely increasing the number of generated options.

Track cost per completed creative or engineering task, not only token price. Astra’s per-token rate is high enough that cache reuse, reasoning effort, long-context thresholds, tool calls, and output length can materially change the economics.

Keep human creative review in the loop for ad variations and product features. The case study itself credits collaboration between Higgsfield’s creative team and engineers rather than presenting Astra as an autonomous replacement for either group.

draft.who_should_care: Teams building AI video products, creative automation platforms, ad-generation workflows, multimodal products, and internal developer tools should care most. The case is particularly relevant to product leaders deciding where a frontier reasoning model belongs in a media pipeline: as a planner, coordinator, coding agent, or creative-direction layer rather than automatically assuming it should generate the media asset itself.
what_to_verify: Measure the exact engineering task Higgsfield’s one-day claim is being compared against before using the result as a productivity benchmark for your own team.

Confirm which model performs each stage of the creative pipeline—planning, copy or concept generation, image work, video generation, editing, evaluation, and final rendering—so Astra’s role is not conflated with the entire stack.
Track reasoning effort, prompt and context size, cached-input reuse, output tokens, tool calls, retries, and human review time when estimating cost per completed feature or creative asset.
Run the same representative workflow with GPT-6 Astra and a lower-cost model such as GPT-6.1 Sol to determine whether Astra’s extra capability changes the final outcome enough to justify the cost.
For ad localization or large-scale variation, define quality and brand-safety checks before increasing the number of generated creative directions.
